study_identification_part.si4_title: Atypical Brain Asymmetry in Autism - A Candidate for Clinically Meaningful Stratification

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To dissect heterogeneity in lateralization in autism using normative modeling, examining individual deviations from normative patterns of brain laterality across age, and to explore associations with clinical symptoms including language delay. The study aimed to move beyond classic case-control analyses to capture individualized patterns of atypical hemispheric lateralization that may serve as clinically meaningful stratification markers.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Subject-specific Z-score images computed at each voxel: Z = (y_ij - ŷ_ij) / sqrt(σ²_ij + σ²_nj), where y is true response, ŷ is predicted mean, σ_ij is predicted variance, and σ_nj is learned population variance. Thresholded at |Z| > 2.6 to define extreme deviations. Extreme rightward (positive) and extreme leftward (negative) deviations summarized per subject as log-transformed percentage of total intracerebral voxels. Alternative thresholding using FDR correction applied in sensitivity analyses.
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The deviation metric is described in mathematical detail in both the main text and supplement, with clear explanation of thresholding and summarization approaches.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: These subject-specific Z score images provide a statistical estimate of how much each individual's true laterality value differs from the predicted laterality value with reference to the neurotypical pattern at each voxel given the participant's age, sex, and site. Normative probability maps were thresholded at an absolute value of |Z| > 2.6. Based on this fixed threshold, we defined extreme rightward-lateralized (positive) and extreme leftward-lateralized (negative) deviations for each participant. All extreme deviations per subject were summarized into (log-transformed) scores representing the percentage of extreme rightward and extreme leftward deviations per subject in relation to the total number of intracerebral voxels.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis:
Answer: General linear models (GLM) tested main effects of diagnosis and sex with age as covariate for percentage of extreme deviations. Effect sizes computed using partial eta squared (ηp²) for ANOVA, Cohen's d for t-tests, and Cohen's φ for chi-square tests. ROI-based analyses extracted extreme deviations within structurally (Harvard-Oxford atlas) and functionally (Neurosynth) defined regions with FDR correction. Relative importance analysis using averaging over orderings method ranked contributions of language delay, ADHD, handedness, sex, and ADOS-2 CSS to explained variance in extreme deviations. Follow-up analyses for language delay included: 1) GLM with LD groups (autism-LD, autism-noLD, neurotypicals), 2) post-hoc t-tests between groups, 3) matched subsample analysis controlling for age and symptom severity. Individual atypicality scores (10% trimmed mean of 1% top deviations) correlated with ADI-R and ADOS-2 symptom scores using 1-tailed Pearson's correlations with FDR correction. Spatial characterization via overlap maps (summing extreme deviations per voxel divided by N subjects × 100). Classic case-control comparison using Permutation Analysis of Linear Models (PALM) examining sex-by-diagnosis(-by-age) interaction with site covariate.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed:
Answer: Using normative modeling of voxelwise gray matter laterality with 10-fold cross-validation, individuals with autism showed significantly more extreme rightward (F(1,580)=12.5, p<.001, ηp²=.021) and leftward (F(1,580)=12.0, p<.001, ηp²=.02) deviations compared to neurotypical controls, with small effect sizes consistent with prior literature. No significant sex differences (right: F(1,580)=0.2, p=.67; left: F(1,580)=0.2, p=.67) or sex-by-diagnosis interactions were found. Classic PALM case-control analysis yielded no significant results, emphasizing the value of individual-level normative modeling. Spatial overlap was minimal across subjects, demonstrating high heterogeneity. Extreme rightward and leftward deviations were positively correlated (r=.41, p<.001). ROI analyses revealed main effects of diagnosis: rightward deviations in frontal operculum (F(1,580)=15.7, p<.001, ηp²=.026), central operculum (F(1,580)=14.9, p<.001, ηp²=.025), and motor network (F(1,580)=9.8, p=.001, ηp²=.017); leftward deviations in superior lateral occipital cortex (F(1,580)=14.4, p<.001, ηp²=.024) and visuospatial network (F(1,580)=11.6, p<.001, ηp²=.02). Sex-by-diagnosis interaction in temporal occipital fusiform cortex (F(1,580)=19.2, p<.001, ηp²=.032) showed females with autism had more extreme rightward deviations. Relative importance analysis (n=305) for extreme rightward deviations (total R²=5.73%): language delay contributed 65.7%, handedness 12.0%, ADHD 11.2%, sex 10.6%, CSS 0.5%. For extreme leftward deviations (total R²=4.56%): CSS contributed 37.7%, language delay 32.2%, sex 13.0%, ADHD 9.7%, handedness 7.1%. Follow-up analyses showed a stepwise pattern for rightward deviations: autism-LD > autism-noLD (t(213)=2.5, p=.01, d=0.32) and autism-LD > NT (t(152)=4.6, p<.001, d=0.58), while autism-noLD vs NT was trending (t(256)=1.9, p=.06, d=0.21). This pattern was more pronounced in males. Rightward deviations in language-related ROIs showed main effects of LD: frontal operculum (F(2,468)=10.6, p<.001, ηp²=.043), central operculum (F(2,468)=7.4, p<.001, ηp²=.03), motor network (F(2,468)=6.9, p=.001, ηp²=.029). Symptom associations: whole-brain rightward deviations correlated with ADI-R communication scores (r=.14, p=.004); in males with autism, rightward deviations correlated with ADI-R social (r=.18, p=.002) and communication (r=.19, p=.001) scores. ABIDE replication showed consistent results: more extreme rightward (F(1,1199)=7.1, p=.008, ηp²=.01) and leftward (F(1,1199)=11.6, p<.001, ηp²=.01) deviations in autism, with no sex differences or interactions. Functional ROI analyses in ABIDE replicated motor network rightward deviations (F(1,1199)=5.2, p=.02, ηp²=.004) and visuospatial network leftward deviations (F(1,1199)=4.0, p=.05, ηp²=.003). Robustness checks confirmed results: with FDR-corrected normative maps (right: F(1,580)=27.1, p<.001, ηp²=0.045; left: F(1,580)=15.1, p<.001, ηp²=0.025), after controlling for FIQ/handedness/SES (right: F(1,387)=7.7, p=.006, ηp²=0.019; left: F(1,387)=4.0, p=.05, ηp²=0.01), excluding intellectual disability (right: F(1,522)=8.8, p=.003, ηp²=0.017; left: F(1,522)=9.3, p=.002, ηp²=0.017), in right-handed only subsample (right: F(1,254)=4.4, p=.03, ηp²=0.017; left: F(1,254)=17.1, p<.001, ηp²=0.063), and in age/symptom-matched LD subgroups (right: F(2,381)=8.3, p<.001, ηp²=0.042; left: F(2,381)=10.5, p<.001, ηp²=0.052).

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes:
Answer: This study demonstrates the clinical utility of normative modeling for parsing heterogeneity in autism and identifying potential stratification biomarkers. The authors suggest that language delay-associated atypical rightward lateralization may constitute a biological marker of etiological subgroups with different language profiles, which has important implications for early prognosis, individualized diagnoses, and language-based interventions in at-risk individuals. Evidence suggests language milestones (onset before age 2 years, level at ages 5-6) predict functional outcomes in autism. The highly individualized patterns of deviations with minimal spatial overlap underscore the need for individual-level rather than group-average analyses. The authors note limited immediate clinical application but suggest future utility in stratifying subgroups with marked deviations and testing associations with outcomes (functioning, persistence, non-psychotic psychopathology). The replicability across LEAP and ABIDE datasets and robustness across multiple sensitivity analyses (ComBat, FDR thresholding, controlling confounds, excluding ID, right-handed only, matched subsamples) strengthen the potential of laterality as a stratification marker. The study represents a step toward precision neuroscience in autism by combining individual-level modeling with careful consideration of multiple sources of heterogeneity (age, sex, handedness, co-occurring symptoms).
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: Clinical implications and application notes are discussed throughout the Discussion section.
Supporting Text: Developing stratification markers based on LD will thus have important clinical implications for early prognosis, individualized diagnoses, and early language-based interventions in individuals at risk... The degree of atypical rightward lateralization may thus constitute a biological marker of different etiological subgroups with different language profiles in autism... through capturing variation at the individual level in combination with addressing different sources of heterogeneity and using a consistent imaging feature in autism, our work provides a step toward precision neuroscience in autism.

caa10_key_limitations.answer:
Answer: Despite large sample size, subsamples become small when stratifying by diagnostic group, sex, language delay, and site, though the Bayesian GPR adapts to data density. Large datasets introduce additional site-related confounds that cannot be fully excluded despite model-based controls and ComBat sensitivity analyses. The cross-sectional design (6-30 years) cannot pinpoint onset and trajectory of atypical development; longitudinal analyses are needed. The normative modeling approach is optimized for detecting extreme deviations but may be less sensitive to the alternative hypothesis that autism involves reduced hemispheric specialization (reduced laterality) rather than extreme deviations. Experience-dependent influences on cortical asymmetry remain unexplored. CV-based correlation maps may be biased; permutation testing was computationally prohibitive. Language delay information was unavailable for ABIDE replication. Sex-specific and detailed age breakdowns for some LEAP subgroups are incompletely reported. Results may not generalize beyond the 6-30 year age range studied.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: Limitations are explicitly discussed in the 'Strengths and Limitations' section of the paper.
Supporting Text: Despite the large dataset, when dividing individuals by diagnostic group, sex, LD, and site, subsamples decrease substantially in size... large datasets come at the expense of additional confounds associated with site... the question arises whether there are also experience-dependent influences on cortical asymmetry. Longitudinal analyses are needed to pinpoint the onset and trajectory of atypical development... the normative modeling approach is suitable for detecting extreme deviations from a normative pattern. However, an alternative hypothesis that individuals with autism might lack specialization of either hemisphere (68), which would be expressed in reduced laterality, might be less detected with the current approach.
Location: Main text lines 170-176; Supplement line 63 discusses CV bias

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The EU-AIMS LEAP dataset was acquired across six sites with different scanners (3T): Cambridge (Siemens Verio), King's College London (GE Discovery MR750), Mannheim (Siemens TimTrio), Nijmegen (Siemens Skyra), Rome (GE Signa HDxTt - excluded after QC), Utrecht (Philips Achieva/Ingenia CX). Acquisition parameters were harmonized: 1.2mm slice thickness, 1.1×1.1×1.2mm resolution, 256×256 coverage. The ABIDE replication merged sites with identical scanners across ABIDE I and II (KKI, NYU, OHSU, SDSU, UCLA1) resulting in 15 total sites. ABIDE images were preprocessed with the same validated laterality pipeline and registered to the LEAP-derived DARTEL template (not a study-specific ABIDE template). Clinical measures: IQ assessed with WASI-II (or WISC-III/IV for children, WAIS-III/IV for adults). ADOS-2 CSS ranges 1-10 (higher = more severe); ADI-R assessed reciprocal social interaction, communication, and RRBs domains plus language development history. Language delay defined as first words >24 months and/or first phrases >33 months. ADHD assessed with DSM-5 rating scale (self- or parent-report); categorical variable: ≥5 positive responses (children) or ≥6 (adults). Handedness from Edinburgh Inventory short version (+500 to -500 scale). SES approximated from annual household income (8-point scale, median £30,000-39,999). The study provides extensive supplementary materials including: detailed preprocessing pipeline diagram (Figure S2), model accuracy maps (correlation/RMSE, Figures S3-S4), sex-stratified normative models (Figure S5), ComBat-based models (Figures S6A-B), site/sex-specific trajectories (Figure S7), FDR-corrected results (Figure S8), matched subsample analyses (Figure S9), handedness/symptom/ADHD breakdowns (Figures S10A-B), ABIDE replication overlap (Figure S11), and comprehensive statistical tables (Tables S1-S3). The paper emphasizes moving beyond traditional case-control analyses to capture individual-level variation and highlights that females with autism showed greater spatial overlap of deviations than males, suggesting less heterogeneity in females. The biological underpinnings of atypical laterality may include genetic factors, prenatal endocrine influences (e.g., androgens), and environmental factors during neurodevelopment, with left frontal regions potentially more susceptible to environmental influences. Full list of EU-AIMS LEAP group members provided in acknowledgments.
